nodes.title: Google Kubernetes Engine: Key Ideas
nodes.content: GKE is GCP's managed Kubernetes service — two flavors: Standard (you manage node pools) and Autopilot (Google manages nodes, you only pay for pod resources). Exam questions test node pools, networking, identity, and which mode to pick.

flashcards.front: GKE Standard vs Autopilot — which to pick?
flashcards.back: Standard: you create and size node pools, pay for nodes whether pods use them or not, full control. Autopilot: Google sizes nodes automatically, you pay only for pods' CPU/RAM/storage, hands-off but less flexibility (e.g., DaemonSets restricted). Pick Autopilot for new projects; Standard when you need GPUs, large nodes, or custom OS.

flashcards.front: What's a node pool?
flashcards.back: A group of nodes with the same machine type, OS, and config inside a GKE cluster. You can have multiple pools (e.g., default + gpu-pool + high-memory-pool). Pods can be scheduled to specific pools via node selectors or taints. Upgrades happen per pool, so prod and batch can be on different K8s versions.

flashcards.front: Workload Identity — why use it?
flashcards.back: Lets a Kubernetes Service Account impersonate a Google Cloud Service Account — pods get GCP IAM permissions without long-lived JSON keys. Replaces the dangerous pattern of mounting `gcp-sa-key.json` as a secret. Always-on by default in Autopilot; opt-in for Standard.

flashcards.front: VPC-native vs routes-based clusters.
flashcards.back: VPC-native: pods get IPs from a secondary range of your VPC — direct routing, no overlay overhead, supports private GKE. Routes-based: legacy, uses GCP routes table (limited to 200 routes per VPC). All new clusters should be VPC-native; routes-based is for legacy compatibility only.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

flashcards.front: What does DNS do?
flashcards.back: Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: You need to allow traffic from the internet to reach VMs on port 443 in your VPC. No current firewall rule exists. What must you do?
choices: Configure a VPC peering link to allow port 443 from internet
Create an ingress firewall rule allowing TCP:443 from 0.0.0.0/0
Assign each VM an external IP and enable IP forwarding rules
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway as the inbound HTTPS reverse proxy
questions.explanation: GCP VPCs use an implicit deny-all ingress rule by default. You must create an explicit ingress firewall rule allowing TCP port 443 from source 0.0.0.0/0 (internet). External IPs alone do not open firewall ports. Cloud NAT is for outbound connectivity only and does not accept unsolicited inbound traffic. VPC peering connects private networks and cannot peer with the public internet.

questions.q: A subnet with no public IPs hosts a fleet of VMs that must reach the public internet for OS updates and SaaS APIs, but must NOT be reachable inbound. The engineer wants a managed regional resource that sources outbound flows on shared NAT addresses without requiring any per-VM public IP. Which GCP resource fits?
choices: Cloud Load Balancer — distributes inbound traffic across backends; does not provide outbound source NAT for private VMs
Cloud Router — exchanges BGP routes between VPC and on-prem networks; not a source-NAT service on its own
Cloud Armor — L7 web application firewall for HTTP(S) load balancers; not relevant to private-VM outbound connectivity
questions.explanation: Cloud NAT (Network Address Translation) allows VM instances without external IP addresses to make outbound connections to the internet while hiding their internal IPs behind NAT IPs. It does not accept unsolicited inbound connections. VPC Network Peering is a separate service for connecting VPCs. Cloud VPN and Cloud Interconnect handle on-premises encryption and connectivity.

questions.q: Which load balancer type should you choose to route HTTP/HTTPS traffic globally to backends in multiple regions with built-in DDoS protection?
questions.explanation: The Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer is a Layer 7 proxy that uses Google's global network to route requests to the nearest healthy backend across regions. It integrates with Cloud Armor for WAF and DDoS protection and supports URL/host-based routing. Internal load balancers serve only private clients. Regional external balancers do not provide cross-region routing.

questions.q: You need to connect your on-premises network to a GCP VPC with dedicated bandwidth of 10 Gbps and low latency. SLAs are critical. Which connectivity option should you choose?
choices: Cloud VPN over the public internet
questions.explanation: Dedicated Interconnect provides a direct physical fiber connection between your on-premises router (in a Google colocation facility) and Google's network, offering 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps links with a 99.9% (or 99.99% with redundant configuration) SLA. Cloud VPN traverses the public internet with no bandwidth SLA. Partner Interconnect goes through a service-provider link. Cloud NAT is an outbound-only service.

questions.q: Which GCP service provides Content Delivery Network caching at Google's global edge locations for HTTP(S) load balanced backends?
questions.explanation: Cloud CDN integrates with the Global External HTTP(S) Load Balancer to cache content at Google's edge points of presence worldwide, reducing latency and origin load. Cloud Armor provides WAF and DDoS protection on the same load balancer but does not cache. Cloud Endpoints manages API contracts. Traffic Director is a managed service-mesh control plane.

questions.q: You are creating a custom VPC network for a new project and choose 'Custom' subnet mode. What does this mean?
choices: GCP automatically creates one /20 subnet in each region for the VPC
Subnets are created manually with explicit IP ranges (no auto subnets)
The VPC uses IPv6 addressing by default on each subnet created in it
Custom mode allows overlapping IP ranges with other VPCs in the project
questions.explanation: In Custom subnet mode no subnets are pre-created. You define each subnet's region and CIDR range manually, giving full control over IP planning. In Auto mode, GCP creates one /20 subnet per region with predefined ranges. Custom mode is recommended for production to avoid range overlaps that would block future VPC peering or hybrid connectivity.

nodes.title: Identity and access management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IAM is the layer that decides who can do what. It's almost always the first thing to misconfigure and the most common security failure mode. Every cloud uses the same primitives — identities, policies, roles — under slightly different names.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.back: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are — password, MFA, certificate. Authorization (AuthZ) decides what you're allowed to do once authenticated — policies, roles, ACLs. AuthN happens first; AuthZ is checked on every request.

flashcards.front: What is a role (vs a user)?
flashcards.back: A user is a long-lived identity tied to a person. A role is a short-lived, assumable identity — services or users 'become' the role to get temporary credentials. Roles let you grant access without sharing long-term keys. Always prefer roles.

flashcards.front: Identity-based vs resource-based policies.
flashcards.back: Identity-based policies attach to a user / role and say what THEY can do. Resource-based policies attach to a thing (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) and say who can access IT. Cross-account access usually needs both: target's resource policy says 'allow this account', source identity policy says 'allow this action on that resource'.

flashcards.front: Why federation / SSO?
flashcards.back: Instead of creating cloud users for every employee, federate from your corporate identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace). Users sign in once with their work account; the IdP issues a SAML / OIDC token; the cloud trades it for temporary credentials. One source of truth, instant deprovisioning.

questions.q: A developer needs to grant a service account the minimum permissions to read objects from a specific Cloud Storage bucket. Which IAM role should be granted at the bucket level?
questions.explanation: roles/storage.objectViewer grants storage.objects.get and storage.objects.list on objects within the bucket without bucket-level administrative permissions, satisfying least privilege. roles/storage.objectAdmin permits write and delete on objects. roles/storage.bucketReader grants metadata read on the bucket itself, not the object data. roles/storage.objectCreator allows uploads only and not reads.

questions.q: You are creating a VM instance that needs to access BigQuery and Cloud Storage without storing credentials on disk. What is the recommended approach?
choices: Copy a service account JSON key onto the VM disk
Set credentials in startup-script env variables
Attach a service account to the VM instance
Use the project's default compute SA with Editor role
questions.explanation: Attaching a service account to a VM instance allows workloads to authenticate to Google Cloud APIs using that service account's identity via the metadata server — no key files needed. Storing key files on disk is a security risk. The default compute service account with Editor is overly permissive. Environment variables in startup scripts are not a secure long-term credential store.

questions.q: An admin needs to grant a role to EVERY member of their Google Workspace organisation in one IAM binding (employees, contractors, future hires alike). They reference a special principal identifier on the binding that resolves to the entire Workspace domain. Which principal identifier is used?
choices: `allAuthenticatedUsers` — every authenticated Google account on the internet, far broader than the company's Workspace tenant
`allUsers` — anonymous public access, even broader than allAuthenticatedUsers; never appropriate for company-only scope
`group:everyone@example.com` — requires creating and maintaining a literal group; not the single-principal mechanism the question describes
questions.explanation: The domain:DOMAIN_NAME principal grants the role to every Google account in a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity domain. allUsers grants access to anyone on the internet, including unauthenticated callers. allAuthenticatedUsers covers any Google-authenticated user globally, not just your domain. group: requires an explicit Google Group to exist and be populated.

questions.q: You need to give an external auditor read-only access to all Cloud Logging entries in your project, including Data Access audit logs. Which predefined IAM role is the minimum that satisfies this?
questions.explanation: roles/logging.privateLogViewer grants read access to all logs including Data Access audit logs, which are treated as private/sensitive. roles/logging.viewer only exposes non-private logs and would hide Data Access entries. roles/viewer is a broad project-level role that exceeds least-privilege. roles/logging.admin grants full control including configuration and deletion, far more than read-only.

questions.q: You need to give a VM in Project A access to a Cloud Storage bucket in Project B. What is the correct approach?
choices: Cross-project access is blocked by default — request a quota change
Share Project A owner credentials with the Project B service account
Grant the VM's service account the required IAM role on the bucket in B
Establish VPC Network Peering between Project A and Project B networks
questions.explanation: IAM bindings can grant any principal — including a service account from another project — a role on any resource. Grant the service account attached to the Project A VM the required role (for example roles/storage.objectViewer) on the specific bucket in Project B. Cross-project IAM is the standard, supported pattern; no quota change or VPC peering is needed. Sharing owner credentials is a serious security anti-pattern.

nodes.title: GCP managed database services: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Google Cloud provides managed databases spanning relational, NoSQL, and globally distributed models. GCP ACE exams test which service fits a given workload and the key trade-offs.

flashcards.front: Cloud SQL vs Cloud Spanner — key difference?
flashcards.back: Cloud SQL: managed MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server for regional workloads. Cloud Spanner: globally distributed, strongly consistent, horizontally scalable — no regional limit.

flashcards.front: Firestore vs Bigtable — choose by workload?
flashcards.back: Firestore: document/NoSQL for mobile and web apps with rich queries and real-time sync. Bigtable: wide-column store for high-throughput time-series or IoT data (no rich queries).

flashcards.front: Cloud Memorystore — what runtimes does it support?
flashcards.back: Managed Redis and Memcached — fully compatible with open-source clients, no patching required, used for caching and session storage.

flashcards.front: When would you choose AlloyDB over Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: AlloyDB is Google's PostgreSQL-compatible database optimised for analytical and transactional mixed workloads; faster than standard Cloud SQL for HTAP use cases.

questions.q: You need a fully managed relational database compatible with MySQL 8.0 on GCP. Which service should you use?
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL is Google's fully managed relational database service supporting MySQL (5.6/5.7/8.0), PostgreSQL, and SQL Server. Cloud Bigtable is a NoSQL wide-column store unsuited to MySQL workloads. Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database but uses its own SQL dialect, not MySQL. Firestore is a NoSQL document database with no relational schema.

questions.q: You need to store structured, schemaless JSON documents with real-time sync for a mobile application. Which GCP database is the best fit?
questions.explanation: Firestore (formerly Cloud Firestore/Datastore) is Google's serverless NoSQL document database with native real-time listeners, offline sync for mobile/web SDKs, and automatic horizontal scaling — purpose-built for mobile and web applications. Cloud Bigtable is for time-series and analytics at massive scale. Cloud SQL and Cloud Spanner are relational databases without document semantics or real-time sync.

questions.q: A Cloud SQL instance is experiencing high read latency under heavy load. You want to offload read queries without changing the application architecture significantly. What should you add?
choices: Upgrade the Cloud SQL tier to a larger machine
Migrate the workload to Cloud Spanner for scale-out
Add Memorystore for Redis as a read-through cache
Add a read replica to the Cloud SQL instance
questions.explanation: Cloud SQL read replicas are asynchronously replicated copies of the primary instance that serve read-only queries; the application only needs to point read traffic at the replica's connection string, no rearchitecture required. Scaling up the primary helps but is more expensive and still a single instance. Memorystore requires application-level cache logic. Spanner migration is a major schema and SQL-dialect change.

questions.q: You need to migrate a 5 TB PostgreSQL database from on-premises to Cloud SQL with continuous replication and minimal cutover downtime. Which GCP service is purpose-built for this?
questions.explanation: Database Migration Service (DMS) provides managed, low-downtime migrations from MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and Oracle to Cloud SQL and AlloyDB. It performs an initial dump and then continuous logical replication so you can cut over with minutes of downtime. Dataflow is for general data-pipeline processing. Data Fusion is visual ETL/ELT. Transfer Appliance is for offline bulk file transfer, not live database replication.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
